Part I — Knowledge Base (English)
Bhaiya's Teachings — Knowledge Base (Session 103, English)
What Is God? The Space Element Teaching, Revisited fr om the Pathshala Session

This session opens with a congr egational sankalp prayer , then r evisits and deepens a question first raised in a r ecent "Pathshala" video: what, concr etely, is God? The speaker walks the gr oup thr ough a series of devotee answers, systematically sets each aside, and arrives at a specific teaching: of the five elements, the space (aakash) element — imper ceptible to sight, sound, or touch — is what this teaching identifies as God, and anything that element "enters" becomes divine. The session closes with a Dhanteras havan announcement.
Part A — Opening and Sankalp

1. Sound check and opening r emarks: The session opens with a brief technical sound check, followed by the speaker's reminder that even in imperfect circumstances (poor audio, discomfort), devotees should stay in a spirit of contentment ("aanand mein raho").

2. The congr egational sankalp prayer: The speaker leads the group in a prayer to Hanuman ji Maharaj, of fering their jaap and sadhna as witnessed by the speaker (referred to by name as "Ashaeiynn ke Parikshit Bhaiya"), requesting inclusion in his sankalp, protection, guidance, and the ability to properly understand the divine's instruction, followed by chanting "Jai Siyaram."

3. Reference to the prior day's Pathshala video: The speaker notes that a "Pathshala" teaching video had been recorded the previous day covering many topics, and states his intent for the whole group to properly understand one topic from it in particular: the nature of divinity and God's existence.
Part B — Testing the Gr oup's Answers to "What Is God?"
1. The opening question: The speaker asks the group directly , "What is God?" and invites answers, deliberately testing and challenging each response rather than accepting the first plausible one.

2. Answers offer ed and set aside: Over the course of the discussion, devotees of fer a wide range of answers — "the supreme formless truth pervading everything," "a source of ener gy ," "the five elements (earth, sky , air, fire, water)," "the supreme soul," "consciousness," "vibration present in everything," "an ener gy with a soul," "the universe itself," "the point where physics and mathematics fail to give an answer ," "one's own inner conscience/intuition," "one's parents (in human form)," and "an entity beyond ordinary human capability ." The speaker probes each in turn, pointing out that most amount to relabeling the question rather than answering it (e.g., "formless" invites the follow-up "formless what, specifically?").

3. A key clarifying exchange — physical vs. astral: The speaker observes that whenever the group discusses God, they instinctively mean the astral world ( एस्टल व�ड�), never the physical world — prompting the question of why that instinct exists.

4. Rejecting "whatever we can't explain is God": One devotee suggests that "whatever we don't understand, we call God." The speaker acknowledges this as close but pushes further , wanting a more precise, mechanistic answer rather than a definition by exclusion.
Part C — The Five Elements and the Case for Space (Aakash)
1. The five elements r ecap: Per this teaching, the five classical elements are earth, water , fire, air, and space (aakash/space element).

2. Four elements can be seen or felt; one cannot: Per this teaching, earth, water , fire, and air can each be directly perceived or felt in some combined form — air felt through wind, water through pressure or touch, fire through heat and light, earth through solid matter — but the space element alone can be neither seen nor felt directly .

3. The cor e teaching — space element as God: Per this teaching, because the space element alone cannot be seen, heard, or felt, and yet plainly exists, it is what devotees are, in practice, always pointing to when they speak of God — not any of the four perceptible elements.

4. "Wherever it enters, that becomes divine": Per this teaching, the space element becoming mixed into or present within any other element or object is what makes that object or place divine — illustrated with examples like holy water , sacred food, or a consecrated murti (idol).

5. Why sacr ed sites and holy water ar e called "divine": Per this teaching, this same principle explains why devotees regard consecrated murtis, holy water , and similar objects as divine — because the space element has entered and mixed into them.

6. How a person becomes closely associated with the divine: Per this teaching, a person whose own space element becomes highly active is one who can perceive and draw upon the astral (spiritual) world more strongly than others — and it is specifically this activation, not any external validation, that leads others to regard such a person as connected to the divine.

7. Subtle chakras and the space element: Per this teaching, the body's subtle chakra system (referred to here as "sookshma chakra") — of which there are seven — is what connects a person to the astral world when it opens; a person with strongly active subtle chakras is described as having a highly activated space element, drawing spiritual ener gies to them accordingly .
Part D — Testing the Framework: The Soldier Who Never Prays

1. The soldier illustration: The speaker introduces a thought experiment: a soldier (illustrated using a "Colonel" figure) who never performs any worship, doesn't know God, and yet is selected out of lakhs of applicants, rises to a senior rank, retires successfully , and has a happy , trouble-free family — with no visible ritual, temple worship, or divine intervention anywhere in the story .

2. The implied question — wher e is God in this story? The speaker poses the puzzle directly: if none of the visible markers of devotion are present, how did this person succeed against such odds? Was the space element/divine element never touched at all?

3. Resolution — it was touched, just unnoticed: Per this teaching, the resolution is that the soldier's space element clearly was activated (since selection against such odds could not otherwise be explained), but this activation went unnoticed and unrecognized rather than being absent.

4. Prarabdha (destiny) and the space element: In response to a devotee's question, the speaker af firms that fate/destiny (prarabdha, bhagya) are themselves concepts that exist entirely within the domain of the space element, since — like the space element itself — they cannot be physically shown, seen, or proven, only explained psychologically . Per this teaching, the
soldier's fortunate outcome is attributed to a space element present in his destiny from childhood, simply never consciously recognized.

5. How the space element becomes "awakened" without formal devotion: Per this teaching, repeating any single activity intensely and consistently enough, over a long enough period, can produce a "saturation point" at which a person becomes so completely absorbed in the activity that their consciousness moves beyond ordinary physical awareness — at that moment, the space element activates and a connection to the astral world begins, independent of whether the activity was religious in nature.

6. "Muscle memory" and astral-body activation: In response to a devotee's comparison to meditation, the speaker agrees that deep absorption in any repeated task (the example given is a soldier's daily long-distance run) can trigger this same state: at a certain extreme point of exertion, the astral body activates, which in turn activates the space element, which then draws in the specific tattva/ener gy associated with that person — and once "hit" in this way , the connection does not fully close again.

7. The soldier's daily run as a r epeated activation ritual: Per this teaching, because the soldier's original activation happened through running, that same activity becomes his ongoing channel back to that state — whenever he needs answers or guidance, running (not conventional prayer) becomes his ef fective route back to the same ener gy , and he returns from it with clarity he would not otherwise have had.

8. Devotion (bhakti) is one path among many , not a r equirement: Per this teaching, bhakti (worship) is explicitly described as merely one available route to activating the space element ("ek zariya"), not a strict requirement — a scientist, architect, or any highly creative, absorbed practitioner can reach the same activation through their own repeated, focused work.
Part E — Consequences of an Activated Space Element

1. "Activation of the space element cr eates miracles": This is of fered as the central, condensed formula of the teaching — a person's activated space element is what produces outcomes that look, from the outside, like divine favor or miracle.

2. What follows activation is itself governed by destiny: Per this teaching, once a person's space element is activated, exactly how that connection develops from there (who comes to them, what support follows, how their fortune unfolds) becomes a further matter of their own individual prarabdha/nasib (destiny/fate) within the space element, not something uniform for everyone.

3. The role of continued jaap: Per this teaching, consistent daily jaap is what keeps a devotee's own space element "portal" open — describing lapses in practice as risking the portal's closure and a resulting decline in overall ener gy and wellbeing (illustrated with the folk saying about a household "band baajna," i.e., misfortune striking, when regular practice is dropped without being either sustained or abandoned outright).

4. A caution against self-blaming over short lapses: In response to a devotee's worry about occasionally missing a day or two of jaap, the speaker reassures that such short lapses are governed by one's own prarabdha and should not become a source of anxiety or self-blame; devotees are encouraged to treat this teaching as knowledge to be studied and researched with curiosity , rather than a source of guilt, since guilt-driven self-focus prevents genuine learning and research into these subjects.

5. Continuous jaap and the space-element "portal": In response to a devotee's question, the speaker confirms that sustained (e.g., 24-hour) jaap keeps the space-element portal continuously open, meaning something can come through at any time during that period — whether the devotee is consciously aware of it in the moment or not.

6. The space element does not discriminate positive fr om negative: In response to a devotee's question about whether negative phenomena also involve the space element, the speaker af firms that the space element itself is neutral — it does not reduce or filter for positive versus negative outcomes, but simply equalizes: what is positive for one person may be negative for another , and vice versa (illustrated with a stock-market profit/loss analogy).

7. Manifestation technique as a space-element practice: In response to a devotee's question, the speaker confirms that repetition-based manifestation practices also work through activating one's own space element, in hopes that a suitable outer force or opportunity arrives to fulfill the manifestation — but cautions that if no such matching force arrives, the intended manifestation may simply fail to materialize despite sincere ef fort.
Part F — Closing Guidance and Announcements

1. Practical daily instruction: The speaker instructs devotees to treat their own space element as their central asset to cultivate — practicing consistently , whatever that practice is, without seeking or fearing external validation, and without turning every setback into self-blame.
2. A caution against public display of devotion: As taught previously , the speaker discourages showy , attention-seeking displays of devotion, encouraging instead quiet, sustained daily practice.

3. The Dhanteras havan announcement: The speaker announces a havan to be held on the evening of the 18th (Dhanteras), at which mantra ahuti (of ferings) will be made using each devotee's own personal mantra; devotees are encouraged to attend and bring family members, and the event is described as intended to strengthen mantra shakti and further activate participants' space element.

4. Purpose of the "jyoti sankalp": In response to a devotee's question, the speaker explains that the jyoti sankalp (lamp-vow) given by Gurudev is primarily aimed at increasing mantra shakti and Vishnu tattva within the body — with the growth of Vishnu tattva described as generally associated with an increase in Lakshmi (prosperity), though the speaker is careful to state this only as a general association, not a direct guarantee.

5. Logistics for the havan — family enr ollment and sutak: In response to devotee questions, the speaker confirms that unregistered family members can be enrolled and have mantra ahuti of fered on their behalf by another devotee present, and that a household observing sutak (a period of ritual impurity , e.g. after a birth or death) should not of fer mantra ahuti themselves that day , though remaining present for the sankalp itself is acceptable.
6. Logistics — attendance flexibility: Devotees with other commitments that evening are told it is acceptable to leave the havan early if genuinely necessary , though full attendance is preferred.
QUICK RULES SUMMARY

Of the five classical elements, the space (aakash) element alone cannot be seen, heard, or felt directly — this teaching identifies the space element as what devotees are actually referring to when they speak of "God." Wherever the space element enters or mixes into another element or object, that object or place is regarded as divine (holy water, sacred food, consecrated murtis). A person becomes closely associated with divinity specifically when their own space element becomes highly active — connected to their body's subtle (sookshma) chakra system. Devotion (bhakti) is one route to activating the space element, not a strict requirement; deep, sustained absorption in any repeated activity (illustrated with a non-religious soldier's daily long-distance run) can trigger the same activation. "Activation of the space element creates miracles" — this is the teaching's core formula for outcomes that look, from outside, like divine favor . What follows activation (who comes, what unfolds) is governed by each person's own individual destiny (prarabdha/nasib), not uniform for everyone. Consistent daily jaap keeps a devotee's own space-element "portal" open; short lapses are governed by one's own prarabdha and should not become a source of guilt or self-blame.

The space element itself is neutral regarding positive and negative outcomes — it equalizes rather than filters. Manifestation practices work by activating the space element in hopes a matching outer force arrives; without such a matching force, the intended manifestation may not materialize despite sincere ef fort. Dhanteras havan (18th, evening): mantra ahuti of fered using each devotee's own personal mantra; family members may be enrolled and have ahuti of fered on their behalf; households observing sutak should not personally of fer mantra ahuti that day .
Part II — Q&A Pairs (English)
Bhaiya's Teachings — Q&A Pairs (Session 103, English)
What Is God? The Space Element Teaching, Revisited fr om the Pathshala Session
User-style questions with answers gr ounded in this session's teaching on the natur e of God and the space element.

Q1. According to this teaching, which of the five classical elements is identified with God? A: The space (aakash) element — per this teaching, it is the one element that can be neither seen, heard, nor felt directly , and is what devotees are, in practice, always referring to when they speak of God.

Q2. Why can't the other four elements be identified with God in the same way , per this teaching? A: Per this teaching, earth, water, fire, and air can each be directly perceived or felt in some combined form (air through wind, water through touch/pressure, fire through heat and light, earth through solid matter), while the space element alone cannot be perceived by any sense.

Q3. What makes an object, place, or offering "divine" in this teaching's framework? A: Per this teaching, wherever the space element enters or mixes into another element or object, that object or place becomes divine — this is of fered as the underlying reason holy water , sacred food, and consecrated murtis are treated as divine.

Q4. What makes a particular person become closely associated with divinity , per this teaching? A: Per this teaching, it is specifically the activation of that person's own space element — connected to their subtle (sookshma) chakra system — that allows them to perceive and draw on the astral world more strongly than others.

Q5. Is devotion (bhakti) r equired to activate the space element, per this teaching? A: No — per this teaching, bhakti is described as one available route ("ek zariya"), not a strict requirement; deep, sustained absorption in any repeated activity can achieve the same activation.

Q6. What is the soldier illustration used in this session, and what point does it make? A: Per this teaching, a soldier who never worships, doesn't know God, yet is selected against long odds, rises in rank, and has a happy life illustrates that his space element was clearly activated — just never consciously recognized as such, since no visible ritual accompanied it.

Q7. How does this teaching explain destiny (prarabdha/bhagya)? A: Per this teaching, destiny is itself a concept existing entirely within the domain of the space element, since — like the space element — it cannot be physically shown or proven, only explained psychologically .

Q8. How can a person's space element become activated without any formal r eligious practice, per this teaching? A: Per this teaching, repeating any single activity intensely and consistently enough can produce a "saturation point" of complete absorption, at which consciousness moves beyond ordinary physical awareness and the space element activates — independent of whether the activity is religious.

Q9. What is the connection between "muscle memory ," the astral body , and the space element, per this teaching? A: Per this teaching, deep absorption in a repeated task (e.g., a soldier's daily long-distance run) can, at an extreme point of exertion, activate the
astral body , which activates the space element, which draws in the tattva/ener gy associated with that person — and once this connection is "hit," it does not fully close again.

Q10. Once activated thr ough a non-r eligious activity , does that activity r emain a person's ongoing channel to that energy? A: Yes — per this teaching, the soldier's daily run remains his ef fective route back to the activated state whenever he needs answers or clarity , functioning much like conventional prayer would for someone else.

Q1 1. What is the teaching's single-sentence summary of what an activated space element pr oduces? A: "Activation of the space element creates miracles" — of fered as this teaching's core formula for outcomes that look, from outside, like divine favor .

Q12. Is what happens after space-element activation the same for everyone? A: No — per this teaching, what follows (who comes to a person, what support arrives, how fortune unfolds) is governed by that individual's own prarabdha/nasib (destiny), not uniform across devotees.

Q13. What keeps a devotee's own space-element "portal" open, per this teaching? A: Consistent daily jaap — per this teaching, lapses risk the portal's closure and a resulting decline in overall ener gy and wellbeing.

Q14. Should a devotee feel guilty about occasionally missing a day or two of jaap? A: No — per this teaching, such short lapses are governed by one's own prarabdha and should not become a source of anxiety or self-blame; the material is meant to be studied with curiosity , not treated as a source of guilt.

Q15. Does sustained (e.g., 24-hour) jaap keep the space-element portal open the whole time? A: Yes — per this teaching, sustained jaap keeps the portal continuously open, meaning something can come through at any point during that period, whether or not the devotee consciously notices it in the moment.

Q16. Does the space element favor positive outcomes over negative ones? A: No — per this teaching, the space element itself is neutral; it does not filter for positive versus negative, but simply equalizes — what is positive for one person may be negative for another , and vice versa.

Q17. How does manifestation practice r elate to the space element, per this teaching? A: Per this teaching, repetition-based manifestation practices work by activating one's own space element in hopes a matching outer force or opportunity arrives to fulfill the manifestation — but without such a matching force, the intended outcome may not materialize despite sincere ef fort.

Q18. What is the stated purpose of the Dhanteras havan announced in this session? A: Mantra ahuti (of ferings) made using each devotee's own personal mantra, intended to strengthen mantra shakti and further activate participants' space element.

Q19. What is the purpose of the "jyoti sankalp" (lamp-vow), per this teaching? A: Per this teaching, it is primarily aimed at increasing mantra shakti and Vishnu tattva within the body; growth of Vishnu tattva is generally associated with an increase in Lakshmi (prosperity), though this is stated only as a general association, not a guarantee.

Q20. Can an unr egister ed family member be included in the Dhanteras havan? A: Yes — per this teaching, they can be enrolled and have mantra ahuti of fered on their behalf by another devotee present.

Q21. Should a household observing sutak (ritual impurity , e.g. after a birth or death) offer mantra ahuti at the havan? A: No — per this teaching, such a household should not personally of fer mantra ahuti that day , though remaining present for the sankalp itself is acceptable.
Bot Response Guidelines

Present the space-element-as-God framework, and the soldier illustration, as this teaching's own devotional/philosophical model — a way of explaining lived experience through this community's framework — not as a claim about physics,

metaphysics, or comparative theology more broadly . When a devotee expresses guilt over lapses in practice, reflect this session's explicit reassurance (Q14) that short lapses are not a cause for self-blame, and that the material should be approached with curiosity rather than anxiety . Do not present the "activation through any repeated activity" teaching (Q8–Q10) as suggesting that non-devotional practice is equally encouraged within Ashaeiynn's own devotional path — it is of fered as an explanatory illustration, not as guidance to replace bhakti with another pursuit. Spelling note: the institute's name is written "Ashaeiynn" — use this spelling consistently .
Part III — Curated Conversational Q&A (Hinglish)
Bhaiya's Teachings — Curated Conversational Q&A (Session 103, Hinglish)
What Is God? The Space Element Teaching, Revisited fr om the Pathshala Session

This is NOT an exhaustive transcript of every exchange in this session. Only conversations judged genuinely valuable and likely to benefit futur e users ar e included, each with a short italicized note explaining why it was kept.
Exchange 1 — "Bhagwan Kya Hai?"

Bhaiya: Main agar aapse poochoon ki bhagwan kya hai? Toh aap kya kahoge? Devotees (various): Param tatva jo sarvavyapi hai... source of ener gy ... bhoomi gagan vayu agni neer ... supreme soul... consciousness... jo cheez humein samajh nahi aati wahi bhagwan hai... Bhaiya: Yeh sab log confuse ho rahe hain. Bilkul basic samjhte hain — na aap gyani na main gyani. Gyani toh hamare Gurudev hain bas.

Why this is her e: Shows the actual back-and-forth Bhaiya used to walk the gr oup thr ough — and past — every common answer befor e arriving at the space-element teaching, useful for anyone wanting to follow the same r easoning pr ocess rather than just the conclusion.
Exchange 2 — The Soldier Who Never Prayed

Bhaiya: Ek fauji jo kabhi puja paath nahi karta, bhagwan ko jaanta bhi nahi... lakhon students mein se paper diya hoga, hazaron mein se select hua hoga. Toh kya uske paas koi shakti nahi hai? Kya uske upar bhagwan ki kripa nahi hai? Devotee: Bhaiya, ismein prarabdh ya bhagya ka role nahi hai kya? Bhaiya: Prarabdh bhagya hai. Prarabdh aur bhagya dono aisi terms hain jinko aap psychologically samjha sakte ho, physically nahi dikha sakte ho na feel kara sakte ho. Toh prarabdh bhagya woh saara space element mein aa gaya.

Why this is her e: The clear est worked example in the session of how this teaching explains appar ent "luck" or success without visible devotion — a question devotees ar e likely to ask again in differ ent wor ds.
Exchange 3 — Havan Logistics for Family and Sutak

Devotee: Bhaiya, jo hum family member ko enroll karva sakte hain, jaise agar mumma registered nahi hai? Bhaiya: Aap karva sakte hain aur unke naam kar sakte hain, woh baithenge, mantra ahuti aap hi doge. Devotee: Aur agar ghar mein sutak ho toh? Bhaiya: Toh sankalp ke baad mantra ahuti na de toh chalega.

Why this is her e: A concr ete, easily-for gotten pair of practical rules for the Dhanteras havan that devotees will likely need to r eference again — enr olling unr egister ed family , and what to do during sutak.
Note on Curation

Most of this session is direct teaching (the space-element explanation and the soldier illustration), which is documented in full in Part I. The exchanges above were chosen because they capture the group's own attempts to answer "what is God," a memorable worked example, and practical logistics questions likely to recur .
